Infrastructure & Security

BTCPay Server Orders Emergency Shutdown After Hot Wallets Swept

Merchants urged to take payment nodes offline immediately as founder Nicolas Dorier links compromises to pre-2.4.2 deployments; exploit underscores the operational boundary of self-custody.

By Staff Reporters · Dispatches from the Relays & Incident Desks

An emergency advisory issued Sunday evening sent shockwaves through the self-hosted payment ecosystem as merchants and node operators were urged to shut down active deployments without delay. We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers. If you're running an instance, please shut it down (./btcpay-down.sh) until we complete the investigation. warned the project's core team [s580]. Core contributor Uncle Rockstar Developer underscored the urgency: Not a drill: shut down your BTCPay Server if you have a hot wallet. [s580]

Merchants moved quickly to bring infrastructure dark. SweetSats confirmed its payment gateway was suspended: PSA: Our BTCPayServer on SweetSats.io is currently shut down until further notice. 🐝 [s61] Operator Nodestrich echoed the alarm: Very serious incident: If you are a BTCPay Server user, please be advised there is an attack under way. ⚠️ [s116] As Psyduck also sounded the alert across social feeds [s19], technical details began to surface from project maintainers.

Preliminary findings shared by founder Nicolas Dorier pointed toward instances running releases prior to version 2.4.2, where attackers obtained administrator access on affected hosts [s580]. Version 2.4.2 had been issued in August to address a vulnerability targeting Lightning nodes, yet the project stopped short of confirming newer builds were unaffected, maintaining a blanket shutdown recommendation. The breach brought renewed scrutiny to the mechanics of automated hot wallets, where signing seeds reside directly on network-connected servers [s580]. As analysts noted in retrospective reviews of the exploit, watch-only configurations where keys reside on offline hardware signers remained isolated from exposure [s580]. Self-custody closes the counterparty risk. It does not close the operational risk. Those are different problems. observed an incident review circulating across long-form feeds [s580].

Custodial Counterparties & Markets

"The Signature Was Valid": Anatomy of the $6.3B Exchange Sweep

Four days after an automated hot-wallet drain emptied balances across ten blockchains, Binance resumes withdrawals while spot bitcoin holds firmly above $78,000.

Four days following the largest single-day balance sheet breach in the history of digital assets, custodial exchange Binance reopened outbound customer withdrawals as market participants assessed structural vulnerabilities in automated signature delegation. In a forensic essay titled The Signature Was Valid, analyst Roger dissected how roughly $6.36 billion vanished across ten blockchains in late October: At 20:04 UTC on Thursday, 29 October, something started moving on the XRP Ledger that should not have been moving. Within twenty minutes the same pattern appeared on Tron, on Bitcoin, and on Ethereum, where a Binance hot wallet authorised a contract to act on its behalf. [s583]

Crucially, investigators confirmed cryptographic private keys were never extracted from hardware security modules. Instead, an intruder who gained lateral access from an internal engineer's laptop instructed trusted service containers to dispatch valid transactions [s583]. Nobody stole the keys. Nobody had to. The attackers found a machine that was allowed to ask for signatures, and the signing infrastructure did exactly what it was built to do: it signed. wrote Roger [s583]. Protocol developers observed that customer claims remain legally enforceable despite internal balance shortfalls. To be accurate, these people did not lose bitcoin they owned. Binance lost their own internal "backing" on IOUs denominated in bitcoin. noted Johnathan Corgan [s33]. Spot exchange rates absorbed the capital flight with unexpected composure, trading at $78,161 on Monday morning [s585], supported by resilient underlying spot liquidity [s561].

Sovereign Architecture & App Releases

Local Relays, FROST Keys, and Autonomous Nodes

Nostr Vault

The architectural dependency on remote relays met a direct alternative with the release of Nostr Vault for Android. Built by developer Logen, the client embeds an entire personal Haven relay and Blossom media server directly onto local handset storage. Most Nostr clients are a window onto someone else's relay. Nostr Vault is the relay. wrote Logen, outlining how outbox notes, encrypted direct messages, and media blobs are committed to local disk before broadcasting outward [s647]. Notifications generate locally without routing through push gateways.

Pomegranate & Verdana

Protocol developer fiatjaf published two architectural tooling releases targeting threshold security and modular computing. Pomegranate introduces FROST key generation, allowing an identity to be partitioned across multiple independent operators so a single compromised machine cannot expose the root identity [s643]. In parallel, Verdana debuted a micro-application framework: Napps are small apps that do one thing and (hopefully) do it well. wrote fiatjaf, detailing portable HTML and WebAssembly runtimes that execute client-side [s644].

Survival LLM & Gertie

Local-first computing expanded into artificial intelligence and developer agents. Calva published Survival LLM, an offline AI assistant pairing lightweight models with emergency medicine and civil defense reference manuals that function without internet connectivity [s640]. For software engineers, Geek introduced Gertie, a native coding-agent harness with GPU rendering and explicit confirmation cards that restrict file system mutations behind permission gates [s648]. Meanwhile, reya announced git backup capabilities in signed to prevent vendor lockouts: i'm developing a feature in signed to help user sync their repo and also all activities to nostr git. [s32]
